item.title: Exploring attentional bias in posttraumatic stress disorder: insights from police officers with service dogs
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction PTSD is characterized by hypervigilance and attentional bias to threat, which can severely interfere with daily functioning. Stress exacerbates this bias by increasing amygdala activity and depleting prefrontal resources, reducing attentional control. The presence of a dog may help regulate attention by reducing stress. Methods This study investigates attentional bias to emotional faces in police officers with PTSD and examines whether the presence of their service or companion dog diminishes this bias by mitigating stress-related cognitive depletion, using a within subject design. Police officers with ( n = 24) and without PTSD ( n = 24) completed the dot-probe task with angry and happy faces in the presence and absence of their dog. Reaction times and event-related potentials (ERP) were analyzed to assess attentional bias. Results Officers with PTSD showed a greater trial level bias score but no consistent bias direction. The P3 amplitude indicated no differentiation between happy and angry faces in the PTSD group, unlike the control group. The VPP amplitude was higher in the PTSD group when the dog was absent, suggesting increased early-stage attention to faces without the dog. Officers with PTSD showed also slower reaction times when their dog was absent. Discussion The findings suggest that PTSD is associated with a reduced ability to selectively allocate attention based on emotional content and increased reaction time variability rather than a consistent directional bias toward or away from emotional stimuli. The presence of a dog appeared to regulate early-stage attentional processing and reaction speed.

item.title: An EMG-driven virtual reality platform for physiology-based motor interaction: technical and functional validation
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Harnessing experience-dependent neuroplasticity has become a central goal of modern neurorehabilitation. Immersive virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool, enabling task-oriented training in ecologically valid scenarios that are difficult to reproduce in conventional clinical settings. Despite these advances, interaction in most existing VR rehabilitation systems remains primarily mediated by external interfaces, such as motion tracking or handheld controllers, rather than by the user’s own physiological motor activity. Consequently, rehabilitation often fails to directly engage the physiological motor commands that naturally drive voluntary movement. We present and validate an integrated VR–electromyography (VR-EMG) platform that enables closed-loop, physiology-driven interaction between users and immersive virtual environments. The platform combines a standalone VR architecture with wearable EMG systems, online EMG decoding, and cloud-based performance monitoring within a unified framework. A standardized motor-command interface enables different EMG acquisition systems to control both anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic virtual effectors without modifying the decoding strategy or rehabilitation scenarios, providing a flexible framework for diverse applications. The platform was validated through complementary technical and functional evaluations performed on the two supported EMG acquisition systems. Technical validation assessed signal quality, gesture classification accuracy, communication latency, and system reliability. Functional validation was conducted in individuals with upper-limb amputation and able-bodied controls while performing object-interaction tasks across multiple immersive virtual scenarios. The platform demonstrated stable closed-loop operation, reliable gesture recognition, and the ability to quantify objective performance metrics, including task score, completion time, gesture classification errors, precision errors, correctly recognized gestures, and user-reported workload. Findings demonstrate the feasibility, technical reliability, and functional versatility of the proposed platform by providing a physiology-driven framework for immersive motor interaction that is compatible with different EMG acquisition systems and dissociates motor control from the morphology of the controlled virtual effector. Because the two systems were used for different components of the validation, we do not establish equivalence in their performance. By integrating online EMG decoding, VR, and quantitative performance monitoring, the platform offers a tool for future applications in rehabilitation, prosthetic training, and studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging and high-density electroencephalography to address whether training with the platform induces changes in functional brain organization.

item.title: Perceived weight status, body image, and depressive symptoms in Korean adolescents: a three-wave longitudinal study and within-person analysis
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Body dissatisfaction is a well-established risk factor for adolescent depression, but two questions remain open. First, it is unclear whether perceived weight status—a subjective cognitive appraisal of one’s body—relates to body image and depression differently from objective body size. Second, most longitudinal evidence relies on between-person models that cannot isolate within-person change. Drawing on a cognitive-behavioral model of body image, we distinguish perceived weight status (a perceptual-categorical appraisal) from body image (the attitudinal-evaluative dimension) and examine both between- and within-person processes. We analyzed three-wave longitudinal data from the Panel Study on Korean Children (ages 13–15; analytic N = 1,148–1,304). A temporally ordered mediation model (perceived weight status at Wave 14 → body image at Wave 15 → depressive symptoms at Wave 16) was estimated using structural equation modeling, controlling for prior depressive symptoms and sex-standardized BMI. Indirect effects were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap resamples with bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals. We examined within-person dynamics using two- and three-variable random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs). Body image was assessed using a refined 4-item scale (α = .735, ω = .77). Perceiving oneself as heavier at W14 predicted a less positive body image at W15 (β = −0.126, p < .001), which in turn predicted higher depressive symptoms at W16 (β = −0.101, p < .001), yielding a small but significant indirect effect (0.013, 95% BCa CI [0.005, 0.025]). Sex-standardized BMI did not significantly predict body image (β = −0.064, p = .091), but the coefficients for perceived weight status and BMI did not differ significantly (Δ = −0.062, p = .368). The indirect effect did not differ by sex (Δ = −0.003, p = .776), although the component paths did. In the RI-CLPM, perceived weight status showed no prospective within-person association with body image ( p = .135) or depressive symptoms ( p = .594). In contrast, body image and depressive symptoms were reciprocally associated within persons (both ps < .01), independent of stable between-person differences. Perceived weight status was prospectively associated with body image, while body image and depressive symptoms showed reciprocal within-person associations. However, the mediational pathway was not supported at the within-person level, suggesting that the observed indirect association may primarily reflect between-person differences. Prevention and intervention efforts may therefore benefit from targeting the reciprocal body image–depression cycle rather than assuming a unidirectional, perception-driven pathway.

item.title: Meditation as a bioactive intervention: evidence of translational potential via Connectivity Mapping and TMS neurophysiology
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Abstract Meditation practices are often used as non-pharmacological adjunct therapy for managing stress and well-being benefits. We propose that beneath their non-pharmacological facade, meditation practices might operate via drug target modulation having profound neurophysiological effects. Firstly, we leverage the Connectivity Map (CMap) to investigate (a) the overlap between meditation-induced molecular signatures and established drug responses, and (b) the pathways and mechanisms contributing to meditation’ potential therapeutic effects. This was studied in a comprehensive temporal RNAseq dataset comprising premeditation, meditation, and follow-up stages from a clinical trial involving 106 participants practising inner engineering meditation. Meditation signatures overlapped with over 438 drugs, but predominantly with drugs targeting the neuroactive ligand receptor pathways, capable of modulating the brain’s excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance. Next, to bridge the meditation-induced molecular changes to measurable neurophysiological effects, we performed a comprehensive meta-analysis of drugs affecting E/I balance through the lens of non-invasive brain stimulation, i.e., transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS-EMG and TMS-EEG). Using multiple correspondence analysis, we then clustered the CMap informed neuroactive drugs and their E/I effects on the same latent space. We found that meditation’s effects mimic drugs targeting the GABAergic, Glutametergic and other neuromodulatory system pathways. Our findings lead to a working model to objectively test neurophysiological changes resulting from meditation that can lead to evidence-based clinical applications. Overall, these findings support the view that meditation acts as a biologically active intervention capable of modulating molecular pathways and cortical excitability, rather than functioning solely as a psychological or contemplative practice.

item.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958–0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
item.description:
Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Digital meditation at scale: a randomized citizen science trial comparing four meditation practices
item.description:
BMC Psychology
This preregistered randomized controlled trial evaluated whether app-delivered meditation improved psychological, cognitive, and physiological outcomes relative to an active control, whether four meditation techniques differed in their effects, and whether individual differences moderated response. A total of 1,211 adults were randomized to four weeks of app-guided loving-kindness, mantra, body scan, or nondual meditation, or to a classical-music active control. Self-report (well-being, mood, self-transcendence, nondual awareness, interoception, compassion), cognitive (Stroop, N-back), and physiological (electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate variability (HRV), heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEP)) outcomes were assessed before and after the intervention and analyzed with linear mixed models and false-discovery-rate correction. No preregistered meditation-versus-control outcome survived FDR correction, and Bayes factors additionally favored the null for the temporal EEG measures. None of the four preregistered technique-specific hypotheses was supported. Two self-report outcomes showed arm differences surviving correction on non-predicted contrasts (self-compassion isolation and sleep quality, both q = 0.050), and mantra participants showed faster working-memory reaction time than body scan participants. The four techniques did not differ from one another. In exploratory moderation analyses, trait neuroticism moderated the meditation effect on working-memory reaction time, with higher-neuroticism participants showing greater benefit in cognitive speed than controls. Four weeks of app-based meditation was not superior to an active music control across psychological, cognitive, and physiological measures, and no preregistered technique-specific hypothesis was supported. The neuroticism finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants replication. Endpoint data were available for 43% of randomized participants and missingness was non-random, which limits inference. This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/xdjfq/overview) on October 24, 2024. International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number, ISRCTN10867561, retrospectively registered on August​ 12, 2026.

item.title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery
item.description:
NeuroImage
Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

item.title: Latent profiles of social-media-specific and general appearance-related characteristics and body-related outcomes
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Appearance-related social media use has been associated with body dissatisfaction and eating-related concerns; however, most studies have employed variable-centred approaches, providing limited insight into how social-media-specific behaviours and broader appearance-related cognitive tendencies co-occur within individuals. Using a person-centred approach, we identified latent profiles defined by social-media content exposure, presentation and validation behaviours, upward appearance comparison, and body surveillance, and examined their concurrent associations with body-related outcomes. Methods A total of 3,504 Greek-speaking adults (66.8% women, mean age = 36.87 years, SD = 10.93) completed a cross-sectional online survey. Latent profile analysis used eight standardised indicators. Distal outcomes were examined using the Bolck -Croon -Hagenaars (BCH) three-step approach, accounting for classification uncertainty and adjusting for age, gender, and body mass index (BMI). Results The analysis supported six profiles: Photo-Manipulation -Focused Users (11.4%), Comparison and Surveillance -Focused Users (16.6%), Exposure-Dominant Users (22.5%), High Appearance-Engagement Users (3.6%), Moderate Appearance-Monitoring Users (24.4%), and Low Appearance-Engagement Users (21.5%). Classification precision was moderate (entropy = 0.710). Profiles differed in appearance satisfaction, drive for thinness, and self-compassion (all p < 0.001). The High Appearance-Engagement profile showed the highest drive for thinness and the lowest self-compassion and, together with the Comparison and Surveillance -Focused profile, the lowest appearance satisfaction. The Low Appearance-Engagement profile showed the lowest drive for thinness and, together with the Exposure-Dominant profile, the highest appearance satisfaction and self-compassion, despite the latter’s elevated exposure. Differences in all three outcomes remained, although attenuated, when profiles were derived from social-media-specific indicators alone. Discussion These findings indicate that distinct configurations of social-media behaviours and appearance-related cognitions are associated with differing body-related outcomes, reflecting heterogeneity that variable-centred analyses may obscure; longitudinal and experimental research is needed to establish temporal and causal relations.

item.title: Changes in negative affect and resting-state EEG power following an EEG-derived generative reality art experience: a pilot pre–post study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Physiological signals are increasingly incorporated into personalized immersive media, but little is known about affective and neurophysiological changes when such signals are used as artistic material. This exploratory pilot study examined an electroencephalography (EEG)-derived generative virtual reality (VR) art experience in which participant-specific EEG signals were symbolically transformed into prompts for immersive visual environments. Thirty healthy university students completed the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule and resting-state EEG recordings before and after a single 5-min experience. EEG analyses examined log-transformed absolute alpha- and beta-band power across frontal, frontocentral, and central regions, with false discovery rate correction. Negative affect decreased from pre- to post-experience (mean change = −3.13, FDR-adjusted p = 0.004), whereas positive affect did not change significantly. Absolute beta-band power decreased across all three regions, and absolute alpha-band power decreased in the frontocentral and central regions (FDR-adjusted p values ≤0.022). Exploratory relative-power analyses showed no significant pre–post differences after correction for multiple comparisons. Frontal alpha asymmetry did not change significantly. Changes in EEG measures were not significantly associated with changes in affect after correction for multiple comparisons. The EEG findings therefore do not establish a neural mechanism for the reduction in negative affect. These findings indicate that the experience was associated with short-term changes in negative affect and resting-state spectral power. Because this pilot study used a single-group design, the findings do not establish causality or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, they provide an initial empirical basis for controlled research on physiological data as personalized material for immersive art and affective experience.

item.title: How Habitual Language Mode Shapes Self-Stigma Perception Process in Deaf Individuals: Evidence from an Event-Related Potentials Study
item.description:
Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience
Deaf individuals often experience public stigma from the hearing majority due to communication barriers, which may further evolve into internalized self-stigma. However, how habitual language mode shapes self-stigma-related processing remains unclear. In the present study, 20 signing deaf and 21 oral deaf individuals completed a semantic priming task while event-related potentials (ERPs) were recorded. Deaf-identity ("I am deaf") primes were presented subliminally or supraliminally before positive and negative trait words. Among oral deaf participants, negative words elicited a larger N400 than positive words under supraliminal priming, while a negative-over-positive LPC effect emerged in the no-priming and subliminal conditions but disappeared under supraliminal priming. Signing deaf participants showed no N400 valence effect but exhibited a negative-over-positive LPC effect across all conditions. These findings provide no clear evidence of self-stigma in either group. Instead, they suggest that habitual language mode and conscious accessibility of deaf identity jointly shape the temporal dynamics of self-evaluative processing, potentially reflecting different ways of resisting the internalization of negative societal evaluations. Signing deaf individuals may derive protection from a culturally and collectively grounded Deaf identity, whereas oral deaf individuals may rely more on individualized, self-protective processing to prevent negative evaluations from being incorporated into the self.

item.title: Neuroergonomic Comparison of User Experience and System Performance for SSVEP-Based Brain Computer Interfaces in Mixed Reality and Virtual Reality Environments
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) deliver high classification accuracy and information transfer rates (ITR), yet their neural responses and user experience vary across immersive display environments. This study compares SSVEP signal characteristics, offline decoding performance, and subjective experience between mixed reality (MR) and virtual reality (VR) head-mounted display (HMD) setups to inform ecologically valid real-world BCI paradigms. Identical visual flicker stimuli (10, 11.25, 15, 18 Hz) were presented via Apple Vision Pro under MR and VR modes. Nine occipito - parietal electroencephalogram (EEG) channels were processed with filter bank canonical correlation analysis (FBCCA) to calculate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), offline classification accuracy (ACC), and ITR. Subjective workload and immersive experience were quantified using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and a customized motion-sickness questionnaire. No statistically significant inter-group difference in grand-averaged SSVEP SNR was detected between MR and VR (F (1,20) = 1.002, p = 0.329). Numerically higher ACC and ITR values were observed for MR (19.51 vs. 18.57 bits/min), but these performance gaps did not reach statistical significance. In exploratory paired comparisons, MR showed lower directional imbalance scores and higher game-experience scores (Z = − 3.431, p = 0.001, r = − 0.75). Across both environments, low-frequency flicker (10, 11.25 Hz) elicited significantly stronger SSVEP responses than high-frequency stimuli (15, 18 Hz, p < 0.001). MR generates consistent SSVEP neural signals alongside favorable subjective perceptual experience, with only non-significant numerical gains in offline decoding efficiency. Key limitations of this work include a small young-adult sample, exclusive offline signal analysis without closed-loop online validation, and inherent optical confounds from differing MR/VR rendering luminance and contrast. These findings provide preliminary offline evidence supporting MR’s usability for home-based rehabilitation and smart-environment BCI applications, while larger-scale online experiments are required to confirm its objective decoding benefits.

item.title: Do autistic traits modulate the neural processing of logical rule violations in visual and auditory modalities?
item.description:
NeuroImage
Similarities in cognitive processing have been reported between individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and non-clinical individuals with autistic traits. However, previous research on autistic traits has primarily focused on social-emotional domains, with limited attention to abstract logical reasoning. Given that sensitivity to rules and patterns is a notable characteristic of the autism spectrum, logical rule processing may be particularly informative for understanding cognitive differences associated with autistic traits. The present research aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural responses of students with autistic traits to logical and illogical number sequences through two event-related potential (ERP) studies. Based on Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10) scores, participants were categorized into High-AQ and Low-AQ groups. In Study 1, both groups judged whether visually presented logical and illogical three number sequences followed a logical incremental rule. In Study 2, both groups performed the same task as in Study 1, except number sequences were presented in the auditory modality. No significant group difference was found in response to logical number sequences in either study. However, relative to the Low-AQ group, the High-AQ group exhibited larger P2 and P3 amplitudes and more negative emotional reactions to illogical number sequences in the visual modality (Study 1), and more positive N1 and LPP amplitudes, and higher arousal ratings to illogical number sequences in the auditory modality (Study 2). These findings suggest that students with autistic traits may exhibit altered neural responses and heightened emotional reactivity specifically to stimuli that violate logical rules in separate visual and auditory studies.

item.title: Screening-positive subclinical eating disorder symptoms and associated factors among high school students: a cross-sectional study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Subclinical eating disorder (SCED) symptoms are common among adolescents and may be associated with adverse psychological and behavioral outcomes. However, evidence on screening-positive SCED symptoms and associated factors among high school students remains limited. Identifying these factors may support early screening and prevention. Methods In December 2023, a stratified random cluster sampling method was used to recruit students from 12 high schools in Yangzhou, Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using a self-developed general information questionnaire, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire 6.0 (EDE-Q 6.0), the Ma Body Figure Scale, the Children’s Depression Inventory–Short Form (CDI-S), the Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale–Short Version (SCAS-S), the National Mental Health Literacy Questionnaire, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. BMI was classified using the WHO 2007 age- and sex-specific BMI-for-age reference for participants younger than 19 years, with adult WHO BMI cut-offs used for participants aged 19 years or older. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) with school as the clustering variable were used to examine factors associated with screening-positive SCED symptoms. Results A total of 2,681 high school students were included in the analysis, of whom 645 (24.1%) screened positive for SCED symptoms. In the school-clustered GEE model, female sex (OR = 1.351, 95% CI: 1.109–1.645), overweight (OR = 3.418, 95% CI: 2.632–4.439), obesity (OR = 7.740, 95% CI: 5.939–10.089), positive body image misperception (OR = 4.280, 95% CI: 3.533–5.184), higher depressive symptom scores (OR per 1-SD increase = 1.454, 95% CI: 1.297–1.630), higher anxiety symptom scores (OR per 1-SD increase = 1.387, 95% CI: 1.269–1.516), and poor sleep quality (OR = 1.393, 95% CI: 1.121–1.733) were associated with higher odds of screening-positive SCED symptoms. Adequate mental health literacy was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.609, 95% CI: 0.506–0.734). Conclusion Approximately one-quarter of the participating high school students screened positive for SCED symptoms. Screening-positive SCED symptoms were associated with weight status, body image misperception, depressive and anxiety symptom severity, sleep quality, and mental health literacy. These findings support multidimensional school-based screening and health education while recognizing that the EDE-Q threshold identifies a screening-defined condition rather than a clinical diagnosis.

item.title: The effect of moral evaluations on the intention to use human augmentation technology: moral considerations as a mediator of personal and societal adoption intentions
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Inroduction Human augmentation technologies (HAT) enhance human abilities through device-based integration or extension of the human body. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) represent a versatile form of HAT, spanning motor, sensory, and cognitive augmentation across a spectrum from restoration to expansion. Although past research identified ethical evaluations as key determinants of HAT acceptance, it remains unclear whether moral evaluations mediate the relationship between technology and user characteristics and usage intentions. This paper examines whether the effects of augmentation-specific (type and purpose of augmentation) and user-specific (disability status) characteristics on personal and societal intention to use HAT are mediated by moral evaluations. Methods We conducted two online experimental vignette studies with German participants. Study 1 employed a 3 × 4 between-participants design ( N = 1,142) with text-based vignettes depicting BCIs varying in augmented ability type and augmentation purpose. Study 2 used video vignettes in a between-participants design ( N = 1,201) featuring workload-adaptive BCIs used by either disabled or able-bodied drivers. We assessed usage intentions via adapted TAM2 scales and moral evaluation via an adapted Multidimensional Ethics Scale. Results Path models show that the effects of augmentation type, augmentation purpose, and user status on personal usage intention were fully mediated by moral evaluations. For societal usage intention, models indicate that moral evaluations fully mediate the effects of augmentation characteristics, and partially mediate those of user status. Discussion These findings indicate that moral evaluations constitute one pathway linking augmentation and user characteristics to BCI acceptance. Overall, this study advances the understanding of ethical aspects in HAT acceptance, using BCIs as an example.

item.title: EEG emotion recognition based on masked generative adversarial networks and neural architecture search
item.description:
User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction
Abstract EEG signals face challenges such as a scarcity of training data, significant individual variability, and difficulties in designing neural network architectures, which severely limit the performance and generalization capabilities of emotion recognition models. This paper proposes an EEG-based emotion recognition method that integrates masked generative adversarial data augmentation with personalized neural architecture search. We designed a data augmentation strategy using a frequency-domain feature-based stochastic electrode mask generative adversarial network, which effectively expands the training dataset and enhances the model’s generalization ability. Subsequently, we constructed a neural architecture search space tailored for EEG signals and employed a differentiable architecture search method to automatically discover the optimal network topology. Finally, a personalized architecture search strategy is employed to independently identify the classification network best suited to each subject’s unique EEG signal characteristics. Experimental validation on the public EEG emotion dataset DEAP achieved a classification accuracy of 98.64% on the Arousal dimension and 98.59% on the Valence dimension, significantly outperforming traditional machine learning methods and deep learning models with fixed architectures.

item.title: Add-on efficacy of neurofeedback-augmented mindfulness training for stress reduction: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Stress is a psychophysiological response that occurs when environmental demands exceed an individual’s coping capacity, and it is closely linked to many psychosomatic disorders. Mindfulness training can effectively reduce stress, but conventional mindfulness training (CM) places high demands on self-monitoring ability, which limits its effect. Neurofeedback-augmented mindfulness training (NM) provides real-time feedback on brain activity signals and may help address this limitation. However, most existing studies are small-sample RCTs, and their conclusions remain inconsistent. This study used a systematic review and meta-analysis to compare the overall effects of NM and CM on stress reduction and related mental health outcomes, aiming to provide evidence-based guidance for intervention selection in non-clinical young and middle-aged populations with mental health needs. We searched MEDLINE, PubMed, Scopus, CNKI, the Cochrane Library, and the ClinicalTrials registry databases. Publication dates were limited to January 2016 to August 2026. Five randomized controlled trials with 358 participants in total were included, and outcomes included stress, anxiety, depression, sleep quality, phone addiction, no-phone phobia, fatigue, neuroticism, and psychological resilience. Extracted data were pooled using a random-effects model, and sensitivity analyses were performed based on heterogeneity. In terms of stress improvement, NM showed a trend toward superiority over CM (SMD 0.65, P = 0.0009), with robust conclusions. For anxiety, two studies comparing NM with CM consistently supported the superiority of NM (SMD 0.67–0.87, both P < 0.01); however, evidence comparing NM with mental health education was inconsistent. For depression, NM showed a trend toward superiority over mental health education (SMD 0.41, P = 0.04), though the robustness was limited; evidence comparing NM with CM was limited and inconsistent. For sleep quality, no advantage of NM was observed compared with either CM or mental health education (SMD 0.05, P = 0.74), and this negative conclusion was robust. For the remaining outcomes, evidence was insufficient or inconsistent, and no definitive conclusions could be drawn. The preliminary evidence from this study suggests that, among non-clinical young and middle-aged adults, NM demonstrated relatively consistent potential advantages in improving stress, with robust directional findings. For anxiety, NM may offer benefits over CM, although the certainty of evidence is limited; evidence comparing NM with mental health education remains inconsistent. For depression, NM may be superior to mental health education, but the robustness is insufficient, and evidence comparing NM with CM is limited and inconsistent. For sleep quality, no advantage of NM was observed, and this negative finding was robust. For the remaining outcomes, definitive conclusions could not be drawn due to the very small number of studies or inconsistent results. These findings are limited by the small number of included studies, the fact that some outcomes were derived from single studies, and the exclusively non-clinical nature of the samples. Further high-quality randomized controlled trials are warranted to verify these results.

item.title: Prosociality differences in neural reward processing during cooperation and competition: an ERP investigation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Reward evaluation is shaped by social context and individual traits, but how prosociality modulates neural gain–loss differentiation during real interpersonal cooperation and competition remains unclear. This study examined the feedback-related negativity difference wave (dFRN) in cooperative and competitive tasks. Methods Forty participants (20 females; mean age = 22 years) completed face-to-face cooperation and competition tasks while EEG was recorded. Prosociality was measured with the Prosocial Scale. dFRN was calculated as loss-evoked minus gain-evoked mean voltage at Fz, FCz, and Cz within 220–300 ms after reward feedback. A 2 (Social Context) × 2 (Prosociality) mixed ANOVA and linear mixed-effects models using continuous prosociality scores were conducted. Results A significant Social Context × Prosocial Trait interaction emerged. High-prosocial participants showed a more negative dFRN in cooperation than in competition, whereas low-prosocial participants showed no reliable context difference. Continuous-score mixed-effects models adjusted for sex supported this association (b = −0.315 μV per scale point, SE = 0.152, z = −2.07, p = 0.039, 95% CI [−0.614, −0.016]); the group-based contrast ( p = 0.054) and robust-standard-error analysis ( p = 0.051) were marginal. Discussion These findings suggest that prosociality is associated with context-dependent reward differentiation, with shared cooperative outcomes eliciting stronger loss–gain differentiation among high-prosocial individuals. Causal interpretation is limited by the fixed task order, differing outcome-generation rules, and unmodeled dyadic dependence.

item.title: Psychological pathways linking body mass index and depression in women and men in a Colombian sociodemographic context
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Body mass index (BMI) shows inconsistent associations with depressive symptoms, and it remains unclear whether body self-esteem and eating disorder symptoms mediate this association, and whether this mediation differs by gender. Therefore, this study used multigroup structural equation modeling to examine these mediators in Colombian young adults, separately for women and men. A total of 662 participants aged 18 to 30 years (398 women, 60.1%; Mage = 21.75, SD = 3.11) were recruited through snowball sampling and completed an online survey with self-reported weight and height and validated measures of body self-esteem, eating disorder symptoms and depressive symptoms. BMI showed no total association with depressive symptoms in women or men. Nevertheless, higher BMI was associated with lower body self-esteem and more eating disorder symptoms, and both mediators were associated with more depressive symptoms, yielding positive indirect effects in women ( b = 0.033, 95% CI [0.022, 0.045]) and men ( b = 0.015, 95% CI [0.006, 0.028]). In men, mediation was indirect-only, whereas in women a negative direct effect offset the indirect effect, a pattern of competitive mediation. The path from BMI to eating disorder symptoms was stronger in women, but the relative weight of the two pathways did not differ by gender. Body self-esteem and eating disorder symptoms link BMI to depressive symptoms in both women and men, with quantitative rather than qualitative gender differences, which suggests that both processes deserve attention in prevention and intervention efforts with young adults.

item.title: A unified fixed-wavelet transformer decodes eight EEG classes across motor imagery, P300, and SSVEP paradigms
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Introduction Motor imagery (MI) can support self-initiated control, whereas brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) based on the P300 or the steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) rely on ongoing visual stimulation. Repetitive visual stimulation can cause visual fatigue; when the stimuli are suspended, however, the corresponding P300 and SSVEP responses can no longer be elicited, and these paradigms alone cannot support a self-initiated command to restart visual stimulation. By contrast, self-initiated MI can provide a voluntary gating signal for switching visual stimulation on or off. Developing a single architecture capable of learning these heterogeneous EEG signatures and decoding multiple user intentions is therefore an important step toward a voluntarily controlled hybrid BCI. Methods To this end, we developed a unified model by extending our previously proposed Analformer, a Transformer-based architecture designed for high classification performance while enabling the analysis of neurophysiologically meaningful EEG representations through AnalNet. We evaluated whether the model could classify EEG trials into eight mutually exclusive classes drawn from MI, P300, and SSVEP paradigms in the OpenBMI dataset. Analformer uses fixed Morlet wavelet kernels to extract frequency-specific EEG features, six Transformer blocks model dependencies across 31 pooled temporal tokens, and a two-stage training procedure to capture both population-level and participant-specific features. Results Across 54 participants, the mean accuracy obtained from the model after participant-specific fine-tuning was 71.00%, compared with 54.53% for EEG-Conformer, 52.30% for EEGNet, and 45.35% for ShallowConvNet under the same evaluation protocol. Ablation analyses showed that replacing the fixed wavelets with learnable convolutions reduced the mean accuracy to 63.15%, whereas omitting the two-stage training procedure reduced it to 47.38%. AnalNet, the built-in analysis module of Analformer, identified class-discriminative patterns, including sensorimotor mu- and beta-band activity during MI and stimulus-locked occipital responses during SSVEP. Discussion Together, these findings indicate that a single Transformer-based architecture can distinguish heterogeneous EEG classes and provide a foundation for unified decoding in hybrid BCIs that combine self-initiated MI gating with P300- and SSVEP-based command selection.

item.title: Simulation-based neural dynamics of stress-related negative cognitive bias in depressive symptoms: a dynamical EEG/ERP framework
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Introduction This simulation-based computational study develops a non-linear state-space framework for stress-related negative cognitive bias and multivariate EEG/ERP observations. Methods A three-state model represents negative bias, cognitive control, and arousal, while symptom load and normalized model stress input reshape a quartic bias potential. N2, P3, late positive potential, frontal theta, frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA), and frontoparietal phase locking provide complementary observation channels. Additional checks distinguish the non-linear benchmark from additive and interaction-only competing generators, examine equilibria of the full coupled system, and perturb the observation model. Results We establish bounded stochastic dynamics, a conditional scalar multistability boundary, stable-branch stress sensitivity, and a sufficient local state-observability condition. A seeded benchmark with 180 simulated participants yields model-implied stress-by-symptom slopes of 66.83 ms for response time, 1.12 μV for LPP, 0.775 dB for frontal theta, 0.133 for FAA, and 0.0769 for frontoparietal PLV. Under a non-linear generating process, mean held-out RMSE was 0.060 for the pre-specified quartic candidate vs. 0.436 for the interaction-only candidate. State-reconstruction RMSE increased from 0.152 under the nominal loading matrix to 0.232 under 15% loading perturbations. Discussion These results demonstrate implementation consistency and characterize model sensitivity; they are not clinical effect estimates or evidence of empirical parameter identifiability.

item.title: “I Know” or “I Feel”? The Impact of Generative AI Applications’ Empathic Response Types on Customers’ Willingness to Forgive
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
As Generative AI (GenAI) increasingly functions as a conversational service agent, human–GenAI interactions involve socioemotional cues such as empathy. Whether customers distinguish qualitatively different forms of GenAI-generated empathy and how these cues shape responses to GenAI service failures remains unclear. Four studies examine how GenAI empathic response type (emotional empathy response vs. cognitive empathy response) shapes customers’ willingness to forgive. Emotional empathy responses (vs. cognitive empathy responses) increase willingness to forgive (Studies 1a and 1b). The effect is stronger for high-severity failures but attenuated for low-severity failures (Study 2a). Study 2b uses event-related potential (ERP) analysis to provide neurophysiological evidence of differential customer responses to GenAI empathic response types. Customers’ emotional experience underlies these differential responses; service failure severity is an important boundary condition. This research deepens understanding of socioemotional interactions in human–computer interaction, showing that customers respond differently to GenAI-generated empathic cues despite GenAI’s lack of genuine emotional experience.

item.title: Comparative EEG analysis of Sutra and Tantra meditations: insights into meditative states and long-term traits
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The Tibetan Buddhist tradition distinguishes between two broad categories of meditation: Sutra and Tantra, which differ in the methods and mental faculties they employ. The main neurophysiological studies of Tibetan Buddhist meditation have been conducted mostly on Sutra practices; while Tantric meditation remains less studied. Methods This publication presents a dual comparative study, using both between-groups and within-subjects design, of the neurophysiological (EEG) correlates characterizing Sutra and Tantra meditative practices, examining both the meditative states and the meditative traits. The study was carried out within the natural environment of Tibetan Buddhist monasteries in India, maintaining the socio-cultural context. Two groups of long-term practitioners (Buddhist monks of Gelug lineage), one experienced in the Tantra tradition (T-group, n = 21) and the other in the Sutra tradition (S-group, n = 20) participated in the study. Results A between-group cluster permutation test revealed that the groups differed in EEG alpha power during meditation, as well as in baseline resting conditions before and after meditation. Specifically, T-group demonstrated consistently lower alpha power compared to the S-group, regardless of the conditions. Thus, the observed differences are stable characteristics of the groups. The within-subjects analysis demonstrated that the conditions (meditation, and baseline resting states before and after meditation) differed only in the T-group: during meditation, an increase in individual alpha peak frequency (iAPF) was observed in the occipital leads, followed by a decrease in iAPF after meditation. Discussion We suggest that reported between-group differences represent enduring meditative traits developed through years of training in meditative techniques in the Sutra and Tantra traditions. Nevertheless, we cannot entirely exclude the possibility that these variations may also stem from certain cohort-specific characteristics unrelated to meditation. An examination of individual power spectra revealed that the absence of significant differences in EEG spectral power between conditions can be primarily attributed to the inter-individual variability in both groups. This variability, in turn, may stem from extensive expertise of highly experienced practitioners, who over years of training, develop individualized cognitive strategies for maintaining the meditative state. Our future research will focus on a more detailed quantitative analysis of inter-individual variability during meditations and on identifying additional between-group differences among practitioners in different traditions.

item.title: Visuospatial attention modulates audiovisual temporal perception: Context-dependent associations between prestimulus alpha lateralization and perceptual reports
item.description:
NeuroImage
Audiovisual temporal perception depends on the timing of sensory events and on preparatory attention. We examined how visuospatial cueing affects explicit synchrony judgments and sound-induced flash illusions, and how prestimulus EEG relates to these perceptual reports. In Experiment 1 (N = 39), participants judged beep-flash synchrony across auditory- and visual-leading stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). In Experiment 2 (N = 36), they reported flashes in fusion and fission conditions across SOAs and corresponding references. Experiment 1 showed a Cue validity × SOA interaction, with more synchrony reports on valid trials at -100 and +50 ms. Cueing shifted the point of subjective simultaneity among 21 participants with reliable fits. Trial-level posterior alpha lateralization was associated with synchrony reports as a function of Cue validity. In Experiment 2, valid cues reduced raw fusion reports at -100, -50, and +100 ms. A Cue validity × SOA interaction persisted for reference-adjusted fusion scores, whereas neither raw nor adjusted fission showed a corresponding interaction. The association between reference-adjusted alpha lateralization and fusion reports varied with Cue validity and SOA, although a direct comparison with the visual reference did not establish an illusion-specific association. These EEG-behavior associations were stable after accounting for temporal progression, preceding trials, cue side, and an ocular-sensitive EEG proxy. Together, the findings indicate timing- and context-dependent effects of visuospatial attention on audiovisual temporal perception and identify preparatory posterior alpha lateralization as a correlate of subsequent reports.

item.title: Neural integration of musical and lyrical emotion: semantic–acoustic congruence in song processing
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Songs convey emotion through the joint contribution of musical-acoustic structure, lyrical semantics, and vocal-prosodic expression, yet these information sources have often been examined separately in affective neuroscience. This Mini Review synthesizes behavioral, electroencephalographic/event-related potential (EEG/ERP), magnetoencephalographic (MEG), and functional neuroimaging evidence relevant to semantic–acoustic emotional congruence during song processing. Available findings suggest that lyrics and melodies engage partially dissociable but interacting processes during song perception. Early MEG responses around 130–140 ms differentiate lyric and melodic expectancy violations in memorized songs, while N400 modulations provide evidence of context-sensitive meaning-related processing across musical and verbal materials. Later positive components may reflect additional attentional allocation and evaluative processing under conflicting or ambiguous conditions, although their functional interpretations remain task-dependent. Functional neuroimaging studies have implicated superior temporal, middle temporal, and inferior frontal regions in lyric–melody processing, whereas studies of music-evoked emotion more broadly have reported activity in the amygdala, insula, cingulate cortex, hippocampus, and striatal regions. The specific contributions of these regions to music–lyric emotional congruence, however, remain uncertain. Behavioral evidence further suggests that congruence does not uniformly facilitate emotional processing and that incongruence may sometimes increase arousal or alter the relative weighting of musical and lyrical cues. On this basis, the review proposes a provisional dynamic weighted-integration account in which musical-acoustic affect, lyrical meaning, and vocal prosody interact across temporally overlapping processing stages, with their relative contributions varying according to expectations, attention, expertise, and language accessibility. Direct neural evidence specifically manipulating music–lyric emotional congruence remains limited, identifying an important direction for future naturalistic and multimodal research.

item.title: Human-Centered, Non-Invasive Brain-to-AI Interfacing (B2AI): A Proof-of-Concept Feasibility Case Study in Augmented Cognition
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Brain-to-AI Interfacing (B2AI) offers a novel human-centered neurotechnology framework for augmented cognition. In this proof-of-concept feasibility case study, we demonstrate a working non-invasive B2AI prototype supporting bidirectional communication between a user and a large language model (LLM) through EEG-based input and TMS-based feedback. In a virtual navigation task, we found that use of the B2AI system was associated with higher path efficiency in a single-user case study. Additionally, we found that the average time per step was higher when the system was active, likely reflecting the time required to initiate the EEG command, query the AI module, receive TMS feedback, and execute the instructed movement. Together, these findings suggest that the B2AI system was technically feasible and may support more efficient task performance under constrained experimental conditions. Future work and fully powered experiments will be needed to determine the generalizability, usability, safety, and application value of the system, but this case study suggests that current technology supports the use of B2AI as an experimental tool for augmented cognition research.

item.title: Neuromorphic Computing in Human-System Interaction: A Scoping Review of Recent Developments, Key Challenges, and Future Research Opportunities
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
This review examines recent advances in neuromorphic computing for human-system interaction (HSI). Inspired by the nervous system, neuromorphic computing utilizes spiking neural network models, event-driven processing, and biomimetic hardware to enable ultra-low power computing. The review analyzes 35 scientific papers published up to May 2026, classifying applications into five categories: brain-computer interface and healthcare applications, human-robot collaboration, neuromorphic synapse and hardware, affective computing and emotion recognition, and neuromorphic sensors and human-machine interfaces. Compared to conventional computing techniques, neuromorphic computing exhibits low-power consumption and faster processing. Recent advancements in neuromorphic computers include the development of memristors, flexible synaptic devices, and self-powered sensory systems. However, challenges such as standardization of datasets, system scalability, hardware-software integration, system explainability, data security, and data privacy can be recognized as the future research topics of neuromorphic computing for HSI. Overall, neuromorphic computing provides a potential HSI solution for a safer, more intelligent, and more human-centered future.

item.title: Exploratory Multimodal Machine Learning for Hazard Response Detection in Semi-Automated Rural Driving
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Partially automated driving systems require drivers to remain cognitively engaged and prepared to respond to unexpected roadway hazards despite reduced direct vehicle control. In rural driving, low visibility and sudden animal crossings pose unique safety challenges to driver readiness and response capability. This study presents an exploratory multimodal machine learning framework for hazard-response classification under semi-automated rural driving. Using a high-fidelity driving simulator, EEG, eye activity, behavioral, and subjective workload data were acquired under manual and Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS)-supported conditions. Pre-hazard event-level features were evaluated using logistic regression, random forest, and multilayer perceptron classifiers with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. Random Forest achieved the highest mean classification accuracy, although performance was constrained by class imbalance and limited sensitivity to brake events. Feature-importance analysis identified SART situation-awareness score as the most influential feature, followed by NASA-TLX workload, pupil-diameter change, and EEG-derived measures. These findings support multimodal hazard-response classification for future driver-readiness modeling.

item.title: Assessment of Static, Dynamic Visual and Multimodal Guidance to Support MI-BCI Paradigm Selection: A Human Factors Comparison
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Sensory cue interface design critically affects the operational performance of motor imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) in rehabilitation and human-machine interaction. Few studies have systematically compared visual and multisensory cues for MI control. This study investigated four cue schemes: static pictures, synchronized visual feedback, visual-audio combination, and visual-vibration combination, with evaluations focusing on BCI classification accuracy and user engagement. The results show that dynamic synchronized visual cues outperform static cues. Additional auditory and haptic stimuli cannot improve but interfere with stable MI performance. Pure synchronized visual cues achieve the most reliable MI control. This study provides ergonomic design guidelines for MI-BCI visual cue layouts.

item.title: Quantifying Shared Mental Models in Nursing Using Multimodal Physiological and Communication Data
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Shared Mental Models (SMMs) are essential for effective nursing teamwork, yet existing assessments mainly rely on observations or self-reports that provide limited insight into team cognition during task execution. This study proposes a multimodal framework for quantifying SMM quality in virtual reality nursing simulations. Thirty nursing students (15 two-person teams) completed three collaborative clinical scenarios while electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and communication data were synchronously collected. Expert annotations were used to classify teams into high- and low-SMM groups. Results showed significant differences in neural activity, visual attention organization, and communication structures between the two groups. High-SMM teams demonstrated distinct EEG patterns, more organized gaze behaviors, and stronger connectivity between task-oriented communication components. These findings suggest that multimodal physiological and behavioral measures can provide objective indicators of SMM quality and support future development of real-time assessment tools for nursing teamwork and simulation-based education.

item.title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener’s own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

item.title: Clinical characteristics, semiology, and comorbidity patterns in non-epileptic seizures (NES): a retrospective comparative study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objectives Non-epileptic seizures (NES) are paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures but not explained by ictal activity. Differential diagnosis may be challenging, particularly because NES and epilepsy can coexist. We aimed to characterize the demographic, clinical, semiological, psychiatric, and instrumental profile of patients with NES, compare patients with NES only with patients with NES epilepsy-only, and assess the robustness of the main associations through sensitivity analyses. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational comparative study using a clinical database from our Neurology Unit (2022–2025) including 38 patients with NES and 23 patients with epilepsy without NES. A total of 18 NES patients had comorbid epilepsy; therefore, the primary comparison included mutually exclusive groups: NES-only ( n = 20) and epilepsy-only ( n = 23). All NES patients were retained for descriptive analyses. Between-group comparisons used exact or non-parametric tests with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) correction. Sensitivity analyses restricted NES-only patients to those with database-recorded video-EEG confirmation and used Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Results Among 38 patients with NES, 94.7% had documented psychological/psychiatric comorbidity, mainly anxiety (50.0%) and depression (28.9%). Positive motor phenomena were documented in 73.7%, neurological examination inconsistency/incongruity in 85.7% of evaluable patients, and video-EEG confirmation in 73.7%. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was significantly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients (90.0% vs. 13.0%; exact OR 50.40, 95% CI 7.29–670.28; BH-FDR p < 0.001), as was anxiety (45.0% vs. 4.3%; BH-FDR p = 0.014). Broad seizure-semiology domains were not significantly different after multiplicity correction. Among imaged patients, abnormal MRI findings were more frequent in epilepsy-only patients (12/18 vs. 0/10; BH-FDR p = 0.006), although MRI ascertainment differed between groups. The psychiatric-comorbidity association persisted in sensitivity analyses. Conclusion NES showed substantial clinical heterogeneity and frequently coexisted with epilepsy. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was markedly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients and remained robust in sensitivity analyses, although differential ascertainment limits interpretation. Broad seizure manifestations alone did not distinguish the groups after multiplicity correction. Instrumental findings should be considered descriptive rather than NES biomarkers. These findings support explicit stratification for comorbid epilepsy and standardized prospective assessment of psychiatric and semiological features.

item.title: CEP-MI: a novel cue-execution dual-stage motor imagery paradigm with PGCANet decoding architecture
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Background Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) holds great potential in neurorehabilitation and motor assistance. Data quality and motor intention decoding effectiveness are closely associated with participants’ engagement. However, previous MI tasks ignored active engagement regulation, and neural mechanisms underlying the transition from motor imagery to execution remain unclear, with limited relevant research. Conventional separate-trial designs cannot capture continuous brain dynamics from imagery to execution and cannot objectively evaluate subject engagement, which hinders mechanism exploration and stable decoding. Methods To address these paradigm-related limitations, a novel cue-execution MI paradigm (CEP-MI) with countdown anchors was designed to quantify engagement. Motor execution sessions were added post-imagery to reveal neural differences during the transition and identify movement-related brain activities. Meanwhile, to boost MI-EEG decoding performance, a collaborative decoding architecture (PGCANet) integrating prior guidance and channel awareness was proposed, with dual branches and consistency constraint loss for decision fusion. Results CEP-MI effectively quantifies participant engagement, and PGCANet achieves superior decoding performance compared to traditional algorithms and advanced models, with the optimal average accuracy reaching 85.77% in binary classification and 82.47% in quadruple classification. Conclusion Targeting the above-mentioned research gaps, the CEP-MI paradigm provides valuable insights into the imagery-execution transition mechanism. PGCANet enhances MI decoding accuracy via multi-branch collaboration, laying a foundation for MI-BCI’s clinical application in neurorehabilitation. Significance This study introduces a novel paradigm and collaborative architecture that significantly advance MI-BCI decoding accuracy and engagement quantification, and helps to promote its clinical application in neurorehabilitation.

item.title: Generative-augmented multimodal neuroaffective decoding for product evaluation: toward neurofeedback-driven human-in-the-loop co-design
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Background Kansei engineering traditionally relies on self-reported evaluations of product impressions, which are susceptible to contextual influences, recall bias, and assessment timing. Multimodal psychophysiological measurements offer complementary insights into affective responses, but integrating heterogeneous signals with limited sample sizes remains challenging. This study proposes Generative-Augmented Multimodal Affective Fusion (GAMAF) to predict perceived attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness in product evaluation. Methods GAMAF integrates feature-space conditional Wasserstein generative adversarial learning with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP), cross-modal attention, graph-based interactions, and adaptive modality weighting. Fifty participants evaluated three automobile cockpit designs, yielding 150 participant–stimulus trials after multimodal quality control. Electroencephalography (EEG), eye tracking (ET), and peripheral physiological signals were integrated and evaluated using nested participant-wise cross-validation. Results GAMAF achieved mean outer-fold R² values of 0.810, 0.850, and 0.840 for attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness, respectively, each with a standard deviation of 0.016. These values exceeded those of the Multimodal Transformer baseline (0.75, 0.78, and 0.76, respectively). Across the three targets, GAMAF reduced aggregate mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) by approximately 29.6% and 29.7%, respectively. Ablation analyses supported the integrated architecture, while adaptive modality weights revealed target-dependent patterns. Discussion GAMAF demonstrates the potential of generative-augmented multimodal fusion for decoding Kansei-related product impressions. However, performance comparisons remain descriptive because baseline variability and participant-level uncertainty were not quantified. Further validation on unseen product designs and closed-loop design optimization is needed to establish its generalizability and practical utility.

item.title: From a surgeon's stroke to a third hemisphere—The auxilium architecture for brain restoration and extension
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
A surgeon was exercising on a stationary bicycle when he had a large ischemic left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, complicated by hemorrhagic transformation requiring hemicraniectomy and cranioplasty. He developed right-sided spastic hemiplegia and a mixed aphasia. This paper takes that case as its anchor to pose the question: beyond improving residual function, what would it mean to restore cognitive function that was lost so that the person fully returns to their pre-stroke baseline? Existing brain-computer interfaces rely on the person having an intact cortical substrate for intended movement and speech. Here we propose the Auxilium, a brain restoration architecture for the situation where that substrate is no longer present: an extracranial auxiliary brain system, agnostic to its substrate, that connects to a person's residual cortex through whatever input-output technology proves most appropriate, and that supplies, in parallel and in real time, new substrate, whether biological or synthetic. We address an assumption of brain-computer interface development, that throughput is the binding constraint. Linking a kHz brain to MHz digital does not impart the higher clock speed, because the limitation lies not in the port but in the architecture of the entire brain and body imparted by evolution. We posit that the substrate of canonical circuits and their integration areas is essential, and the Auxilium can be understood as restoring both connectivity (linkage between disconnected areas) and computation (information generation capability of a volume of neural tissue). We propose a near-term de-risking pipeline using stereoelectroencephalography during surgical epilepsy evaluation, comparing extracranial modules spanning threshold rules, PID controllers, expert systems, artificial neural networks, neuromorphic devices, and biological specimens, each linked in real time to a participant serving as their own control on naturalistic tasks. If ports alone restore the lost function, the requirement is routing connectivity. If performance improves only when the module supplies its own dynamics, the requirement is computational substrate. We expect the answer to depend on how much tissue was lost, how quickly, and on the individual's reserve, and we treat routing and substrate as endpoints of a continuum to be mapped empirically.

item.title: Data-driven subgroups of adolescent depression: integrating EEG-derived brain networks, childhood trauma, and depressive symptoms
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Abstract Background Adolescent major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity and heightened sensitivity to psychosocial adversity, particularly childhood trauma. Ongoing neurodevelopment and brain plasticity during adolescence may limit the applicability of adult-derived neurobiological models. Previous studies have rarely integrated large-scale network connectivity, trauma exposure, and symptom dimensions within a single multivariate framework and have largely relied on functional magnetic resonance imaging or univariate electroencephalographic (EEG) measures. Methods This cross-sectional case-control study included 67 medication-free adolescents with MDD and 35 matched healthy controls. Resting-state source-space EEG functional connectivity was estimated. Sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) was used to identify multivariate associations between network connectivity and clinical and childhood-trauma measures. Moderation analysis examined whether network connectivity moderated the association between trauma and depression severity. K-means clustering of sCCA-derived canonical variates was used to identify data-driven patient subgroups. Results Adolescents with MDD showed lower default mode network (DMN)-limbic network (LMN) connectivity than healthy controls. The only sCCA mode meeting the prespecified robustness criteria linked physical abuse, emotional neglect, and anxiety/somatization to distributed connectivity features, particularly those involving the frontoparietal, limbic, visual, and salience networks. Within-visual-network connectivity moderated the association between childhood trauma and depression severity. Clustering identified two patient subgroups with distinct symptom and network profiles. Conclusions EEG-derived network measures may help characterize the interplay between childhood trauma and clinical heterogeneity in adolescent MDD. These preliminary findings require replication in larger, independent samples. Clinical trial number not applicable

item.title: Real-Time Vigilance Monitoring via Biosignals: A Scoping Review
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
This scoping review aims to identify types of computational models that use physiological signals for real-time vigilance monitoring. Vigilance, or the ability to sustain attention over time, is essential in domains such as driving, aviation, and industrial operations, where lapses can cause serious harm. Following PRISMA guidelines, the review searched IEEE, ProQuest, PubMed, and ScienceDirect and identified 16 studies that examined vigilance and real-time monitoring systems. Most studies applied supervised machine learning, mainly for binary classification of vigilance states such as alert versus drowsy, and were concentrated in automotive contexts. Electroencephalography (EEG) was the most commonly used sensor, while heart rate variability (HRV), electrooculography (EOG), photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) appeared less frequently. Overall, current systems still prioritize threshold-based detection over continuous tracking of vigilance changes. The review highlights the need for multimodal sensing, real-world validation, and adaptive modeling frameworks to support reliable deployment across diverse operational environments.

item.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces for AAC: Hybrid SSVEP + Eye-Tracking for Faster Selection Rates
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Augmentative and alternative communication systems are essential for people with severe speech and motor impairments, yet many interfaces remain slow, effortful, and error-prone. This study evaluated a hybrid brain-computer interface that combines steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEP) with eye-tracking to improve selection speed, reliability, and usability. Participants completed symbol selection, short phrase construction, and correction tasks under three conditions: SSVEP-only, eye-tracking-only, and hybrid SSVEP plus eye-tracking. In the hybrid condition, gaze rapidly narrowed the likely target region, while SSVEP classification confirmed user intent. Outcomes included selection rate, accuracy, errors, correction time, communication throughput, workload, effort, trust, and preference. The hybrid interface achieved the strongest performance, with faster selection than SSVEP-only and better control than eye-tracking-only. It also reduced accidental selections and correction burden, particularly in dense layouts and longer tasks. Results further emphasized personalized gaze thresholds, SSVEP windows, and visual layouts for sustained, practical AAC use across diverse user needs.

item.title: Between-group differences in resting-state functional connectivity within the brain’s extended triple-network following genuine and sham chiropractic adjustments: a quasi-experimental pilot trial
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
